overview:
Mauritius is a small island nation in the Indian Ocean, about 2,000 kilometers off the southeast coast of Africa and east of Madagascar. The main island, ringed by coral reefs and white beaches, is about the size of Rhode Island, and the country also includes Rodrigues and several tiny outer islands. The capital, Port Louis, is a busy harbor city with a colonial-era market, skyscrapers, and a racecourse that is one of the oldest in the world.

About 1.3 million people live in Mauritius, and they are a true mix: descendants of Indian laborers, African slaves, Chinese traders, and French and British settlers live side by side, and Hindu temples, mosques, churches, and pagodas stand within blocks of each other. English is the official language of parliament, French dominates the media, and Mauritian Creole is what everyone speaks at home. Mauritius is a stable parliamentary republic and one of Africa's wealthiest and best-governed countries, earning its living from tourism, sugar, textiles, and financial services.
landAndNature: Mauritius was born from a volcano that rose from the sea about eight million years ago and is now extinct; its jagged peaks, like Le Morne Brabant and the three-fingered Trois Mamelles, are its worn remains. A central plateau of sugarcane fields and tea gardens slopes down to a coast almost entirely enclosed by coral reef, creating calm turquoise lagoons. At Chamarel, the Seven Colored Earths are dunes of sand in stripes of red, brown, violet, and blue. Black River Gorges National Park protects the last native forest, home to the pink pigeon, the echo parakeet, and the Mauritius kestrel, all rescued from the brink of extinction. The dodo, a flightless bird found only here, was wiped out within a century of humans arriving. The climate is tropical, with cyclone season in summer.
peopleAndCulture: About two-thirds of Mauritians are of Indian origin, and Hinduism is the largest religion, followed by Christianity and Islam, so the calendar is packed with festivals: Diwali lights up homes, Cavadee sees devotees carry decorated arches, Chinese New Year brings dragon dances, and Christmas falls in summer. Food blends everything: dholl puri flatbreads stuffed with split peas, Creole rougaille tomato stew, Chinese fried noodles, and French pastries, often eaten at street stalls. Sega, a dance and music born among enslaved Africans, is performed to the beat of the ravanne drum with swaying hips and bare feet on the beach, and is recognized by UNESCO. Soccer is popular, and horse racing at Champ de Mars draws big crowds.
history: Arab and Malay sailors knew the island, but it was uninhabited when the Portuguese arrived in the early 1500s. The Dutch settled in 1638, named it after Prince Maurice of Nassau, cut down its ebony forests, and left in 1710; by then the dodo was extinct. France took over in 1715, brought enslaved Africans to grow sugar, and built Port Louis. Britain captured the island in 1810 and, after abolishing slavery in 1835, brought about half a million laborers from India to work the plantations, shaping the nation's makeup. Mauritius became independent on March 12, 1968, and a republic in 1992. It has been a peaceful democracy ever since. Mauritius still claims the Chagos Islands, which Britain separated before independence.
funFacts: The dodo, a flightless bird found only on Mauritius, went extinct less than a century after humans arrived, around 1680.
The Mauritius kestrel numbered only four birds in 1974 and was saved by breeding programs, becoming a conservation legend.
Mauritius issued some of the world's most valuable postage stamps in 1847; a single Post Office stamp has sold for millions.
The Champ de Mars racecourse in Port Louis, opened in 1812, is the oldest in the Southern Hemisphere.
The Seven Colored Earths at Chamarel never mix, even after heavy rain, because the sands settle back into separate stripes.
